title: I Took the Pasta-Extruder Die Checkout to the Baker Who Left My Semolina

parts.text: I stepped into bench two at 11:06 a.m. and baker Nico was already using my numbered die. The board said: SIXTY MINUTES. DIES STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty, kitchen steward, holding a clipboard that listed our run. Nico shrugged. "Bakers keep the hopper." I photographed the board, the booking, and his dough in my hopper. Then I asked for the die checkout. At 11:14 the kitchen desk pinged why Nico's dough sat in our hopper. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The kitchen desk can see Nico's dough in the hopper during our run.

social.video_title: He left my semolina in the numbered die — Part 1/2
social.description: Community pasta bench, a baker in my hopper, a sixty-minute clock he posted. I logged the dough. Would you have asked for the die checkout?

parts.text: Nico called it test dies until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the hopper still. The die went back to my numbered drawer. Nico ran a slot of their own and told the next baker atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: BAKERS DO NOT KEEP THE HOPPER. I keep our run on a labeled card. Nico brown-bags his dough. The bench finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.
